specAnchors.text: know and use the relationship between efficiency, useful energy output and total energy output: efficiency = useful energy output ×100% total energy output
describe a variety of everyday and scientific devices and situations, explaining the transfer of the input energy in terms of the above relationship, including their representation by Sankey diagrams

primer.text: Efficiency turns the conservation law into a score: of all the energy leaving a device, how much served the purpose? This note fixes the equation, works a fan motor from 300 J to 72%, and teaches Sankey diagrams — the arrow picture where widths are joules and efficiency is visible at a glance.

modules.title: Efficiency and the efficiency equation
sourceHeadings: What is efficiency in an energy transfer?
modules.opening: Efficiency scores an energy transfer: what fraction of the output actually serves the purpose? It is the useful share of the output expressed as a percentage — and conservation of energy pins the total output to the total input, with the wasted share filling the gap.
keyPoints: Efficiency scores how much of a transfer is wasted.
High efficiency means most of the transferred energy is useful; low efficiency means most is wasted.
By conservation of energy, what leaves equals what arrives.
The output splits into the useful share plus the wasted share.

low.restatement: Efficiency is a percentage score: useful output over total output, where the total equals the input by conservation and the wasted share fills whatever the useful share leaves.
low.analogy: A goalkeeper’s save percentage: saves (useful) divided by all shots faced (total output) — the rest conceded (wasted).
low.examPointer: Write the equation with × 100% for a percentage, or without it for a ratio between 0 and 1 — match the form the question asks for.

medium.restatement: The arithmetic chain is fixed: total output = total input (conservation), useful output = total output − wasted, then divide useful by total and scale by 100 for the percentage.
medium.analogy: A pay slip: gross pay (input) arrives, tax and pension (wasted) are deducted, and take-home (useful) divided by gross is the efficiency.
medium.examPointer: Efficiency above 100% is impossible — that claim is a favourite true-or-false check and conservation is the reason.

modules.title: Sankey diagrams
modules.opening: A Sankey diagram draws an energy transfer as arrows whose widths are proportional to the energy they carry: one flat input arrow entering, the useful output running straight on, and the wasted output bending away. Because energy is conserved, the widths always recombine to the input width.
keyPoints: A Sankey diagram draws an energy transfer as splitting arrows.
The flat left-hand end is the energy arriving at the system.
The straight arrow to the right represents the useful energy output.
The arrows bending away represent the wasted energy.
Arrow width is proportional to the energy transferred, and total energy in equals total energy out.

low.restatement: Read a Sankey left to right: input width in, straight arrow = useful output, bent arrows = wasted output, and the widths always sum back to the input because energy is conserved.
low.analogy: A river delta: the main channel carries the useful flow onward while side channels bleed away — wider channels mean more water, or here, more joules.
low.examPointer: Widths are PROPORTIONAL, not equal — exam questions test whether you read the arrow widths as energy amounts.

medium.restatement: The three parts of the diagram map exactly onto the three quantities of the efficiency equation: input, useful output and wasted output; conservation is the reason the widths close the balance.
medium.analogy: Splitting a pizza on a plate: the whole pizza arrives (input), the slices guests take are useful, the crumbs on the table are wasted — and nothing left the plate unseen.
medium.examPointer: Learn the two splitting-point equations: total in = total out, and total in = useful out + wasted out.

modules.title: Sankey diagrams of light bulbs and the lifting motor
modules.opening: Two bulbs drawing the same input make the efficiency lesson visible: the modern bulb keeps its straight arrow wide while the filament bulb bleeds most of its width into heat. The lifting-motor diagram then shows the arithmetic every Sankey can be reduced to: waste = input − useful.
keyPoints: A Sankey for a modern efficient bulb looks very different from an old filament bulb’s.
A more efficient bulb has less wasted energy, shown by a smaller downward heat arrow.
The of-record motor Sankey shows 500 J in and 120 J out usefully.
Wasted = total in minus useful out: the motor’s Sankey reads 500 J in and 120 J out usefully, so 380 J is wasted by subtraction.

low.restatement: Same input, different split: the efficient bulb’s Sankey keeps most width in the straight useful arrow, the filament bulb’s bends most of it away as heat; the motor example turns the widths into 380 J wasted and 24% efficient.
low.analogy: Two funnels of the same mouth: the good one pours almost everything into the bottle, the leaky one dribbles most of it down the outside.
low.examPointer: The Sankey arithmetic move: wasted = total energy in − useful energy out (500 − 120 = 380 J in the of-record example).

medium.restatement: Sankey questions end in one of two calculations: read the widths as joules and subtract for waste, or divide useful by total for the percentage; both rest on the widths being proportional.
medium.analogy: Reading a stained-glass window: the pane widths tell the story without a single number, but a ruler converts them to data when asked.
medium.examPointer: Efficiency from a Sankey = useful width ÷ input width × 100; quote the widths in your working.

glossary.definition: The ratio of the useful energy output from a system to its total energy output, usually as a percentage.
The share of the output energy that serves the intended purpose.
The share of the output energy that does not serve the intended purpose.
A diagram of an energy transfer whose arrow widths are proportional to the energy transferred.

workedExample.prompt: The blades of a fan are turned by an electric motor. In one second, 300 J of energy is transferred electrically from the mains supply and 85 J is wasted due to friction and sound. Calculate the efficiency of the motor.
steps: List the known quantities: total energy input = 300 J and total wasted energy = 85 J.
State the equation: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy output × 100%.
By conservation of energy, total energy output = total energy input = 300 J.
Useful energy output = total energy output - wasted energy = 300 - 85 = 215 J.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The efficiency of the motor is 72% (215 J of every 300 J is useful).
